summary: Addresses PSAP callback after emergency calls, so a call taker's callback is not blocked by authorization policies or sent to an answering machine, within the IETF emergency services architecture. It builds on the IETF's emergency services work.

eli5.summary: When you call for help and get cut off, the helper must be able to call back and get through.

questions: how to ensure emergency callbacks get through
what is the sip psap-callback priority value
why do emergency callbacks get blocked
subtitle: A SIP marker that lets an emergency call taker's callback get through call barring and forwarding.

tldr.problem: After an emergency call ends, the call taker may need to call back, but the callback looks like any other call and can be blocked, forwarded or sent to an answering machine. The existing domain-matching approach fails in several deployments.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7090 defines a new value, psap-callback, for the SIP Priority header field to mark a PSAP callback. Providers honor it only if the PSAP's identity matches a white list, and user agents only within a timer after the original call.
tldr.outcome: Networks and phones can give marked callbacks better treatment, while unrecognized or unverified markings fall back to normal call handling. What preferential treatment means is left to local policy.

facts.label: Scenarios covered
facts.value: 5, with PSTN interworking out of scope

today: RFC 7090 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Callbacks Get Lost
sections.content:
When an emergency call is set up, the call taker's user agent receives the caller's address-of-record (AOR) and, if available, a Globally Routable User Agent URI (GRUU). Regulators require enough information to let the call taker call back if the call drops or more communication is needed. That attempt is called a PSAP callback.

The problem is that SIP proxies and phones cannot tell a PSAP callback from any other call. Features such as call barring, do not disturb and call diversion (call forwarding) may block it or send it to an answering machine. These features can live in intermediaries as well as in the user agent.

The emergency community wants better odds of reaching the caller, while making sure other calls cannot slip past the same filters.
sections.eli5: Your phone is good at ignoring strangers. That is a problem when the stranger is the emergency helper calling you back, because the phone cannot tell the difference.

sections.title: The Existing Mechanism and Its Limits
sections.content:
Section 13 of RFC 6443 already says a user agent may treat a call as a PSAP callback if it comes from the same domain as the PSAP that answered the earlier emergency call, is directed to the supplied Contact header or AOR, and arrives within a reasonable time. RFC 6881 suggests 30 minutes.

This works like a stateful packet-filtering firewall. It is simple, but it needs call state in the user agent and in SIP intermediaries, and it breaks whenever the callback comes from a different domain or passes through a different proxy than the outgoing call did.
sections.eli5: The old trick is to remember who you called and let them ring back. It fails if they call from a different building than the one you reached.

sections.title: Scenarios Where Matching Fails
sections.content:
The RFC walks through five cases where the stored state does not match the callback.

  • Routing asymmetry: a VoIP provider uses different proxies for inbound and outbound calls. State is created at the outbound proxy, but the callback arrives at the inbound proxy.
  • Multi-stage routing: the call goes through an ESRP (Emergency Service Routing Proxy) before the final PSAP. The provider stored the ESRP's domain, but the callback comes from the PSAP's domain.
  • Call forwarding: the call enters one emergency network and is forwarded to others, so the callback comes from a domain other than the one stored.
  • Network-based service URN resolution: the provider resolves the service URN to a PSAP URI, so the provider's state is right but the user agent's is wrong.
  • PSTN interworking: there is no guarantee that the callback leaves through the same gateway or uses the same endpoint identifier.

The PSTN case is declared out of scope, and the specified solution does not support it.
sections.eli5: Imagine you phone one office, but the answer comes back from a different desk or building. Your doorman only expected the first office, so he turns the call away.

sections.title: The psap-callback Priority Value
sections.content:
The RFC adds one new value, psap-callback, to the SIP Priority header field from RFC 3261. It tells SIP entities that the request belongs to a PSAP callback session.

Entities that see the value in an initial request for a session can, depending on local policy, apply PSAP-callback-specific procedures. Both network entities and the callee may do so. The actual actions, such as bypassing services and barring procedures, are outside the scope of the document.

The syntax is a single ABNF extension of priority-value.
sections.eli5: It is a special stamp on the call that says this is the helper calling you back. What your phone does with the stamp is up to its own rules.

sections.title: Preventing Abuse of the Marker
sections.content:
A marked call can bypass blacklists and call forwarding, and a user agent that supports the value could override settings such as vibrate-only mode. Any SIP entity, including an attacker, can insert the indicator. So the mechanism must not be usable for purposes such as telemarketing, and an unrecognized, unverified or ignored marking must not break call handling: the call is treated as if it had no marking.

The RFC splits the defense between proxies and user agents.

  • Proxies and providers: a VoIP provider MUST give preferential treatment only when the PSAP's calling party identity matches an entry in a white list of valid PSAPs. If there is no match, it MUST remove the marking so the callback becomes a normal call. Identity can come from SIP Identity (RFC 4474), P-Asserted-Identity (RFC 3325) or TLS between neighbors. Keeping the white list may be operationally complex, and is easier when the provider and PSAP operator already have a relationship.
  • User agents: a UA that made an emergency call MUST keep state so it can accept a callback within a reasonable time, with a timer started when the original call ended. It does not need the calling party identity, since the callback may use a different one. The timer, such as 30 minutes per RFC 6881, also stops providers from misusing the marker, for example to make their support calls reach customers.
  • Same media: a PSAP callback MUST use the same media as the original call. A person with disabilities may need a certain medium, and a caller who chose text may be hiding from someone who would hear a voice ringtone.
sections.eli5: Anyone could forge the stamp, so the phone company checks the sender against a list of real emergency centers. Your phone also only listens for a short time after your call, and the helper must use the same way of talking that you used.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA is asked to add the psap-callback value to the SIP Priority Header Field Values registry that was created by RFC 6878. Its semantics are those described in the section on the indicator.
sections.eli5: The new stamp gets written into the official list of allowed stamps so everyone uses the same name.
